title: Longest common subsequence: subsequence enumeration vs dynamic programming
problem_statement: Given strings a and b, compute the length of the longest string that is a subsequence of both.

input.parameter: n = length of each string (|a| = |b| = n in the harness).

algorithms.name: subsequence enumeration
algorithms.idea: Enumerate all 2^n subsequences of a and test each against b with one greedy scan.
algorithms.pseudocode: for each subset S of positions of a: if a[S] is a subsequence of b: best = max(best, |S|)
algorithms.correctness: Exhaustive; the greedy leftmost-match scan decides the subsequence relation exactly.

algorithms.name: dynamic programming
algorithms.idea: L(i, j) = L(i-1, j-1) + 1 if a_i = b_j, else max(L(i-1, j), L(i, j-1)); fill the table row by row.

relationship: Exponential enumeration of candidate subsequences is replaced by a quadratic table of prefix-pair subproblems.

sources.authors: Cormen, T. H.; Leiserson, C. E.; Rivest, R. L.; Stein, C.
sources.title: Introduction to Algorithms (3rd ed.)

sources.authors: Wagner, R. A.; Fischer, M. J.
sources.title: The string-to-string correction problem

sources.authors: Abboud, A.; Backurs, A.; Vassilevska Williams, V.
sources.title: Quadratic-Time Hardness of LCS and other Sequence Similarity Measures

verification.method: V1: both agree on random DNA-alphabet string pairs (n <= 12 for enumeration). V2: runtimes fitted against 2^n n and n^2.

caveats: Conditional lower bound: no O(n^(2-eps)) algorithm unless SETH fails (Abboud-Backurs-Vassilevska Williams).

lower_bounds.bound: no O(n^(2-eps)) algorithm for any eps > 0
lower_bounds.setting: conditional on the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH)
